column1: # Quoting is removed before the rules see a word.
# A run-time value is any text: it carries an allow only where the rule's
# wildcard covers it and no guard could match it.

column2: echo repos/x | xargs -I{} gh api -X{} repos/x

column1: # zsh decides these itself, so they stay with Claude: a parameter flag,

# a function, and a statement that sets the shell's search path.

column2: for f in a b; do rg -n x $f; done

for m in -XPOST; do gh api $m repos/x; done

column1: # A literal assignment that always runs, and is the only one, fixes the
# value; one that may be skipped, repeated, or kept in a subshell does not.
# cd to a known directory moves where later commands, redirects and git run.
# git, after cd or with -C, takes a directory shaped like a bare repository
# (`bare` holds HEAD, objects and refs; `linked` holds HEAD and a commondir
# naming bare; `dotgit` is bare beside an empty `.git`) as one and runs its
# config, so that asks; any other directory, such as the repository
# `bare/work`, is judged like the working one.
# A rule that starts with `*` is about the script's text, such as a variable
# it names, which no run-time value adds; a bare assignment is text too.
# A word that starts with literal text other than `-` and cannot split, a
# glob like `src/*` or a plain `src/$f`, expands only to words that start
# with that text, so no option deny such as `rg * --pre *` can match it. A
# bare glob or value, or an unquoted $(…), still may: in a program that ends
# its options at `--`, that is denied with the advice to use one. A word
# starting `-` is an option `--` would not move, so it stays with Claude.
# Git reads settings only from -c and --config-env before its subcommand,
# from `git config`, and from a transport URL, so a text rule such as
# `git*core.pager*` cannot be met by a value after another literal
# subcommand. A rule about the subcommand's own
# An `export` of harmless variables to literal values changes nothing a rule
# decides; `setopt` of the options a plain `set` may change neither.
# After a literal `--`, a program that ends its options there reads run-time
# words as operands, so an option guard cannot meet them; a path guard still
# may. $TMPDIR, like $HOME, is fixed for the whole script.
# A redirect reads or writes a file, judged by the Read and Edit rules: a
# write needs an Edit allow, a read an allow or a working directory, and a
# matching deny or ask decides the command.

column1: # Symlinks: the file the shell opens is judged. `escape` leads outside every
# allowed tree, `inner` into the extra working directory, and `env-link` is
# a dangling link to .env that writing through would create. /tmp is
# Arithmetic over numbers, and variables bound to numbers, is only a number;
# zsh evaluates a variable's value as math too, so an unknown one, or an
# operator that assigns, stays with Claude.

column2: for i in 1 2; do echo $((i + 1)); done

column1: # hyperfine is judged by every script it times or runs around them, from
# where it runs, and by the files --input reads and --export-* writes.
# $(mktemp) with no template, -t or an absolute one names a fresh file in
# a known directory ($TMPDIR is {extra} here); a relative template does not.
# A failed mktemp prints nothing: after `;` the variable may be empty, so
# `cd $D` goes home, and inside a longer word the rest stands alone.
# A git rule for another subcommand cannot meet the run-time words after a
# built-in one; after an alias, which may stand for any subcommand, it can.
# uv run starts its literal target with every later word as an argument, so
# a rule for another target cannot meet them; one for the same target can.
# A loop over a plain glob runs over the names it matches when the hook runs,
# from the directory the script is in, as zsh expands it: each pass is judged
# with its name, so git -C meets every directory, bare ones included. No
# match, or an unknown directory, leaves the variable any text.

column2: for d in ex*/; do rg -n x "$d"; done
for d in */; do git -C "$d" status; done
cd {extra}/.. && for d in */; do git -C $d status; done
for d in nomatch*/; do git -C "$d" status; done
(cd bare); for d in */; do git -C "$d" status; done
for d in {root}/ex*/; do rg -n x $d; done
for d in "$PWD"/ex*/; do rg -n x "$d"; done
cd {root} && for d in "$PWD"/*/; do git -C "$d" status; done
for d in "$x"/*/; do git -C "$d" status; done
